title: CHAPTER THIRTY-ONE. On the necessity and contingency of things
latin: CAPUT TRICESIMUM PRIMUM, De necessitate et contingentia rerum. NECESSITAS est divinae potentiae influxus dans rebus modum, quo ita sunt ut aliter esse non possint. Omnes enim appellant necessarium id quod non potest aliter se habere. Quod autem non potest aliter se habere, id necesse est ita se habere ut habet. Quod autem sic est et non aliter esse potest, id vel non aliunde est, ut Deus, ens primum et independens, de quo supra vidimus, vel a causis rerum est. II. Est autem vel a fine, vel ab agente, vel ab idea, vel a materia, vel a forma.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): II. But it is either from ye end, or from ye agent, or from ye idea, or from matter, or from form. or it is from ye causes belonging toward things — as God, ye first plus independent being, concerning whom we saw above — that which is so plus cannot be otherwise is either not from elsewhere. it is necessary that it so hold itself as it holds — But what cannot hold itself otherwise. For all call necessary that which cannot hold itself otherwise. NECESSITY is ye influx belonging toward divine power giving things a mode by which they so are that they cannot be otherwise. CHAPTER THIRTY-ONE. On ye necessity plus contingency belonging toward things.
english: CHAPTER THIRTY-ONE. On the necessity and contingency of things.

NECESSITY is the influx of divine power giving things a mode by which they so are that they cannot be otherwise. For all call necessary that which cannot hold itself otherwise. And what cannot hold itself otherwise must so hold itself as it does. And what is so and cannot be otherwise is either from nowhere else — as God, the first and independent being, of whom we treated above — or is from the causes of things.
II. And it is either from the end, or from the agent, or from the idea, or from matter, or from form.

title: III–V: necessity of end, of agent, and of idea
latin: III. Necessitas finis est duplex, vel simpliciter vel ad melius. Sic ad salutem, iuxta concionem Evangelii, fides necessaria est simpliciter: notitia vero linguarum sanctarum et lectio sacrarum litterarum propter melius, quia sine illa nemo servatur; sine his servatur, etsi non ita bene. IV. Necessitas ab agente itidem duplex est, violenta et naturalis. Violenta, ut cum epulo ille evangelicus rapitur in gehennam contra voluntatis suae inclinationem. Naturalis, cum spiritus epulonis a sono musico movetur, quia natura mobilis est spiritus et a sono invitatur ad propriam operationem. Ex parte vero violenta et ex parte naturalis est necessitas cum lignum aridum ignitur, quia quatenus aridum est a calore dispositum ad plus caloris recipiendum, quatenus vero lignum est, contra naturam eius est comburi. V. Necessitas ex idea est, qua secundum ideam Dei aut hominis res ita se habent ut aliter habere nequeant. Hinc enim est quod duo et tria faciunt quinque, et numerus usque ad denarium progreditur apud nos, non autem apud omnes nationes. Nam non transit senarium apud quosdam Afros. Hinc etiam litterae et syllabae apud hanc aut illam gentem ita formantur et non aliter. Et haec necessitas concurrit quodammodo cum formali: sed quia potest se aliter habere ad placitum artificis, unde aliae nationes alias litteras et alia vocabula habent, idcirco non est necessitas intrinseca ut formalis.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): therefore it is not intrinsic necessity as formal — whence other nations have other letters plus other vocabularies — but because it can hold itself otherwise toward ye artisan's pleasure — plus this necessity concurs somehow with formal. V. Necessity from idea is that by which according toward God's or humankind's idea things so hold themselves that they cannot hold otherwise. IV. Necessity from ye agent is likewise double, violent plus natural. III. Necessity belonging toward ye end is double, either simply or toward ye better — faith is necessary simply toward salvation according toward ye Gospel's preaching.  Simply necessary toward salvation according toward the Gospel preaching is faith alone whereas knowledge of the holy languages and reading of sacred letters are toward the better because without faith nobody is saved but without those helps one may still be saved though not so well. Violent necessity appears when that rich man of the Gospel is dragged into Gehenna against his will inclination while natural necessity appears when his spirit is moved by musical sound because spirit by nature is movable and invited by sound toward its proper operation. Dry wood kindled shows necessity partly violent partly natural inasmuch as dry it is disposed by heat to receive more heat yet inasmuch as wood to be burned is against its nature. Necessity from idea explains why two and three make five and why number progresses to ten among us yet not among all nations for among some Africans it does not pass six and why letters and syllables are formed thus among this or that people and not otherwise. This necessity concurs somehow with the formal yet because it can hold otherwise at the artisan pleasure whence other nations have other letters and vocabularies it is not intrinsic necessity as the formal is.
english: III. Necessity of the end is twofold: either simply, or unto the better. So unto salvation, according to the preaching of the Gospel, faith is necessary simply; but knowledge of the holy languages and reading of the sacred letters are unto the better — because without faith no one is saved; without these one is saved, though not so well.

IV. Necessity from the agent is likewise twofold: violent and natural. Violent, as when that rich man of the Gospel is dragged into Gehenna against the inclination of his will. Natural, when the rich man's spirit is moved by musical sound, because spirit is by nature movable and is invited by sound to its proper operation. And necessity is partly violent and partly natural when dry wood is kindled — inasmuch as dry it is disposed by heat to receive more heat, but inasmuch as wood, to be burned is against its nature.

V. Necessity from idea is that by which, according to the idea of God or of humankind, things so hold themselves that they cannot hold otherwise. Hence two and three make five, and number progresses to ten among us, yet not among all nations — for among some Africans it does not pass six. Hence also letters and syllables are so formed among this or that people and not otherwise. And this necessity concurs somehow with the formal; but because it can hold itself otherwise at the artisan's pleasure — whence other nations have other letters and other words — therefore it is not intrinsic necessity as the formal is.

title: VI–VII: material and formal necessity; necessity of supposition; only God simply necessary
latin: VI. Necessitas materialis est, quae a rei materia divinitus determinata dependet. VII. Necessitas formalis est, quae a forma rei dependet. Utraque a nonnullis dicitur absoluta, item essentialis, secundum quam compositum omnino non potest aliter se habere. Sic necesse est hominem esse animal rationale. Quae vero res determinata materia carent, ut numerus, triangulus, circulus, qui in ligno, lapide et ubique fieri possunt, non habent a materia necessitatem, sed ab idea sola. Sic necessario est homo carne et ossibus praeditus necessitate materiae; necessario rationalis est necessitate formali, quia forma est actionum et operationum principium. Et ex hac necessitate essentiali oritur necessitas in syllogismis. Unde sequitur omnem necessitatem a primo necessario esse, sicut numerus ad unitatem, et omnis potentia passiva ad activam respicit. Voluntaria omnia necessaria sunt necessitate naturali, non violenta. Cum volumus, necessario volumus — necessitatem suppositionis, quae evenit e statu rei, non a conditione. An omnia excepto Deo necessitatem suppositionis participent? Nulla videtur esse necessitas quae non sit suppositionis, excepta divina. Deum enim esse potentissimum, sapientissimum et optimum necessarium est absoluta necessitate. Sed hominem esse animal rationale necessarium est supposita voluntate Dei decernentis facere hominem huius essentiae. Unde prisci quidam theologi non inepte in solo Deo ponunt necessitatem simpliciter; in ceteris vero secundum quid.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): whence certain ancient theologians not unfitly place necessity simply in God alone; but in ye rest according toward something. But that humankind is a rational animal is necessary with God's will supposed deciding to make humankind belonging toward this essence. For that God is most powerful, most wise plus best is necessary by absolute necessity. Excepting ye divine, no necessity seems to be which is not belonging toward supposition. When we will, we necessarily will — ye necessity belonging toward supposition. VI–VII. Material necessity depends from ye thing's matter divinely determined; formal from ye form. Both by some are called absolute, likewise essential.  Material necessity depends from a thing matter as divinely determined while formal necessity depends from the form and both by some are called absolute likewise essential according to which a composite cannot hold itself otherwise at all. So it is necessary that humankind be a rational animal yet things lacking determined matter such as number triangle circle which can be made in wood stone and everywhere have necessity not from matter but from idea alone. Humankind is necessarily endowed with flesh and bones by necessity of matter and necessarily rational by formal necessity because form is the principle of actions and operations and from this essential necessity arises necessity in syllogisms. Every necessity is from the first Necessary as number looks to unity and every passive power to the active. All voluntary things are necessary by natural necessity not violent and when we will we necessarily will which is necessity of supposition arising from the thing state not from a condition. Excepting the divine no necessity seems to be which is not of supposition for that God is most powerful most wise and best is necessary by absolute necessity but that humankind is a rational animal is necessary with God will supposed deciding to make humankind of this essence. Whence certain ancient theologians not unfitly place necessity simply in God alone and in the rest only in a qualified sense.
english: VI. Material necessity is that which depends on a thing's matter as divinely determined. VII. Formal necessity is that which depends on the thing's form. Both are called by some absolute, and likewise essential, according to which a composite cannot hold itself otherwise at all. So it is necessary that humankind be a rational animal. But things that lack determined matter — as number, triangle, circle, which can be made in wood, stone, and everywhere — have necessity not from matter but from idea alone.

So humankind is necessarily endowed with flesh and bones by necessity of matter; necessarily rational by formal necessity, because form is the principle of actions and operations. And from this essential necessity arises necessity in syllogisms. Whence it follows that every necessity is from the first Necessary, as number looks to unity, and every passive power to the active.

All voluntary things are necessary by natural necessity, not violent. When we will, we necessarily will — the necessity of supposition, which arises from the thing's state, not from a condition. Do all things except God share the necessity of supposition? No necessity seems to be that is not of supposition, except the divine. For that God is most powerful, most wise, and best is necessary by absolute necessity. But that humankind is a rational animal is necessary with God's will supposed deciding to make humankind of this essence. Whence certain ancient theologians not unfitly place necessity simply in God alone, and in the rest only in a qualified sense.

title: VIII: contingency as withdrawal from the necessary; plurality, motion, disformity
latin: VIII. Haec de necessitate: CONTINGENTIA est recessus a necessario, quo res ita sunt ut aliter esse possint. Contingens est quidam a necessario recessus, et necessarium consistit in uno, contingens vero in pluribus, ac dicitur tot modis quot necessarium. Unde Caietanus 1.1. quaest. 13 artic. 13 ait, contingens habere rationem pluralitatis, motus ac disformitatis, quia potest aliter se habere: necessarium vero unius et uniformis, quia impossibile est aliter se habere. Contingens vero a necessario procedit naturaliter, ut pluralitas ab unitate, et non e converso.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): plus not conversely — as plurality from unity — But ye contingent proceeds from ye necessary naturally. because it is impossible to hold itself otherwise — ye necessary belonging toward one plus ye uniform — because it can hold itself otherwise — ye contingent has ye reason belonging toward plurality, motion plus disformity — Whence Cajetan 1.1 question 13 article 13 says. plus it is said in as many modes as ye necessary — plus ye necessary consists in one, but ye contingent in many. CONTINGENCY is a withdrawal from ye necessary, by which things so are that they can be otherwise. VIII. These things concerning necessity.
english: VIII. So much concerning necessity: CONTINGENCY is a withdrawal from the necessary, by which things so are that they can be otherwise. The contingent is a certain withdrawal from the necessary; and the necessary consists in one, but the contingent in many, and it is spoken of in as many modes as the necessary.

Whence Cajetan (Summa I, question 13, article 13) says that the contingent has the character of plurality, motion, and disformity, because it can hold itself otherwise; but the necessary has the character of one and of the uniform, because it is impossible to hold itself otherwise. And the contingent proceeds from the necessary naturally, as plurality from unity, and not the reverse.

title: Future contingents; how God knows them; Cap. 31 close toward fate
latin: I. An futura contingentia aliquo pacto sub scientia Dei cadant? Affirmandum est. Deus enim cognoscit res contingentes ut sunt, quia, ut sunt, necessario sunt, quomodocunque sint. Scientia Dei non imponit rebus necessitatem absolutam, sed respicit eas ut in suis causis et in aeterno decreto. II. Duo modo Deus futura contingentia cognoscit: in seipsis, quatenus praesentia sunt aeternitati ipsius, et in suis causis, quatenus decrevit ea producere vel permittere. Plura qui volet, legat post scholasticos in locis Philippi Melanchthonis locum de causa peccati et contingentia. Sic necessitas potentiae, fatum sapientiae, harmonia amoris praeparant transitum ad caput de fato.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): thus necessity belonging toward power, fate belonging toward wisdom, harmony belonging toward love prepare ye passage toward ye chapter concerning fate. let who wills read after ye scholastics in Philip Melanchthon's loci ye place concerning ye cause belonging toward sin plus contingency. II. In two modes God knows future contingents: in themselves inasmuch as they are present toward his eternity, plus in their causes inasmuch as he decreed to produce or permit them. because as they are they necessarily are, however they may be — For God knows contingent things as they are. I. Whether future contingents fall under God's knowledge by some pact? It is to be affirmed.
english: I. Do future contingents fall under God's knowledge in any way? It is to be affirmed. For God knows contingent things as they are, because as they are they necessarily are, however they may be. God's knowledge does not impose absolute necessity on things, but regards them as in their causes and in the eternal decree.

II. God knows future contingents in two modes: in themselves, inasmuch as they are present to His eternity; and in their causes, inasmuch as He decreed to produce or to permit them. Whoever wants more, let him read after the scholastics in Philip Melanchthon's Loci the place on the cause of sin and on contingency. So necessity of power, fate of wisdom, and harmony of love prepare the passage to the chapter on fate.
